newsitem.title: USA: U.S. copper market steady, but supply loosening up.
newsitem.headline: U.S. copper market steady, but supply loosening up.

text.p: U.S. copper is still buoyed by decent demand, but it was too early to say if current good metal supplies stemmed solely from holiday shutdowns or were a sign of gathering surpluses, traders and producers said.
"Most of current demand is being met from current production," a physical trader said. "The good business we saw in the fourth quarter is continuing into the first quarter."
Another trader added, "I don't believe there is any problem with supply."
The large 11,475-tonne LME stock hike Tuesday was mainly in Singapore, with some traders dismissing it as a "one-off" event.
Tuesday, most-active March COMEX copper rose 2.20 cents to 103.70 cents a lb by noon EST/1700 GMT.
"Singapore is unpredictable and just depends on people nobody knows much about," the physical trader said.
An East Coast brass mill executive added, "The interesting thing is what happens when people come back to work. That's going to give you your real long-term answer."
Spot business was said to be fairly quiet with January bookings all concluded and another week or so to go before February orders are placed.

Combined COMEX and LME stocks in the United States remained largely unchanged in recent months despite the switches in inter-exchange premiums causing metal to flow from COMEX to LME and then back again.
Traders said much of the flow between rival exchanges' warehouses had dried up for the time being because nearby LME and COMEX contracts were roughly even, leaving little arb trading opportunities.
But U.S. supplies may ease further this quarter as Kennecott Utah Copper was scheduled to finally bring up to full capacity its 310,000 short tons per year smelter.
Still, Kennecott remained cautious and its spokeswoman Alexis Fernandez said modifications to the problem-hit plant were continuing.
"We are not coming out with any detailed figures until the first quarter production figures come out," Fernandez added.

Scrap, however, is becoming more plentiful as sustained higher cathode prices have lured more secondary metal out of the woodwork. As a result, scrap's discount to cathode has widened a touch, merchants said.
"I think we will see people trying to maybe get away from cathodes and refined due to their closer relationship with COMEX prices," a Midwest scrap merchant said.
Some consumers had been using more cathode and less scrap because the price of the latter was so strong.
Exports of copper scrap have also eased as China enters its New Lunar Year holiday period, thereby helping to boost domestic availability.

And China's insistence since November that scrap merchants pay an inspection fee to guarantee the quality of each container exported has had an negative effect. "It's affecting our business - it's making us hesitant and not necessarily making us competitive," a West coast scrap exporter said.
But one unknown which still lingers in the background is the outcome of protracted labor talks at Phelps Dodge Corp's Chino mine in New Mexico.
Workers at the 168,000 ton per year facility have been without labor contracts for the past six months, and no new dates have been set for fresh talks, a Phelps spokeswoman said Monday.
((Huw Jones, New York Commodities 212-859-1646))
